7	### THE CENTRAL STORY: Ostrey Hollow milk-testing station and the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association
8	
9	#### Geography / entities
10	- **Larrow Valley** — the valley; contains **Larrow Green** (site of the main creamery, on Larrow Creek, built 1891) and, seven miles up-valley, **Ostrey Hollow**, at the head of which stood the **skimming station**.
11	- **Hessel Bottom** — a wet meadow below the Ostrey Hollow hamlet; the best milk in the Hollow came from here. Seven farms had grazing/haying rights on Hessel Bottom (per r02/Effie Loomis) — but Roy Brant (r09) says **six farms**; the largest was **Emmet Brant's** (per r02) — confirmed independently by Roy Brant (r09): the Brant farm was "the largest of the six — sixty-odd acres of the meadow, and thirty-eight cows in a good year." "Six farms" is corroborated by FIVE independent sources (r09, r15/Grigg's 1908 committee report, r16/Kepp, r17/Hazel Brant, plus the underlying 1908 report itself) against r02/Loomis's lone "seven." r19 (Ashlin Chronicle) independently reaffirms "six farms."
12	- **Ashlin** — the county seat/town where hearings, the Association's office (later), the historical society, and legal business took place. Per r17: the Brant weigh book was held "down the street at the historical rooms in this town" of Ashlin. Per r18/Duncan Keddie: the Brant weigh book went to the "Ordell County Historical Rooms" in Ashlin in 1963 (given by Hazel Brant); the station test book also went there in 1959. r19 confirms "Ordell County" again. The newspaper is **The Ashlin Chronicle**, a county weekly, front page, dated 3 October 1958.
13	- **Farland** — site of a college with a library (where Ivy Keddie later worked/taught/studied, and where Merle Strawn's notebooks were held). The State Agricultural College at Farland published Bulletin No. 214 (1911, feeding trial on bog hay) and Bulletin No. 471 (1958, final exoneration), co-authored by Professor Leland Vaught and Miss Ivy Keddie.
14	- **Redlow Ridge**, **Vessey County** — location of the **Alder Corners Cheese Company** (a rival/comparison creamery, used for cross-checking milk tests). Per r10 (Rosalie Cudd): the ridge is a 4-mile switchback road, cut for a lumber road, shuts in November and does not open before April (some years May).
15	- **Tarnet** — home city of **Ammon & Sons**, "a dairy supply house," per r17/Hazel Brant the place the pipette crate "came out from... in ninety-nine" (1899). Confirmed by r19 as Ammon & Sons' home city, from whom the Association's testing outfit was bought new in 1897 for $77.39 (six dozen pipettes, test bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight), going into use spring 1897. Junia Ammon, the firm's own historian, writing "Sixty Years of Ammon & Sons" (1949, ch. 9), confirms Tarnet as the firm's home city on the street behind the railroad yard — a four-story building plus base]

## Section A — Reconstruction: the last two of the eight stories

I don't know where Batches 1–2 drew their story boundaries. Based on the internal chronology, the most natural eight-way division of the Ostrey Hollow saga runs: (1) founding of the Association, (2) the station's opening and its own glassware arriving, (3) early operation and first complaints, (4) the 1908 wet-hay investigation, (5) the 1911 broken-measure episode, (6) the 1919 circular and the Brant rift plus the 1923 glass condemnation, (7) the 1925 arbitration and dismissal, (8) the 1958 discovery, exoneration, and the scattering of the documents. If Batches 1–2 covered (1)–(6), these are (7) and (8) — the two that come last in time. Flagging this assumption explicitly since I can't verify it.
